Consider the initial value problem above. By applying the Laplace transform to both sides of each equation, find the system of equations." :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the Laplace transforms of both sides of each equation in our system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}L\{{x}_{1}^{′}(t)\}=L\{2{x}_{1}(t)+5\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-3\} \\ L\{{x}_{2}^{′}(t)\}=L\{-3{x}_{1}(t)+4{x}_{2}(t)+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the derivative property of the Laplace transform, we obtain the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}sL\{{x}_{1}(t)\}-{x}_{1}(0)=2L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}+5L\{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\}-3L\{1\} \\ sL\{{x}_{2}(t)\}-{x}_{2}(0)=-3L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}+4L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}+2L\{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the results

$$
\mathcal L\{1\} = \dfrac{1}{s}, \quad
\mathcal L\{\cos(2t)\} = \dfrac{s}{s^2+4}, \quad
\mathcal L\{\sin(2t)\} = \dfrac{2}{s^2+4},
$$

we can write our system as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)-1=2{X}_{1}(s)+\frac{5s}{{s}^{2}+4}-\frac{3}{s} \\ s{X}_{2}(s)+2=-3{X}_{1}(s)+4{X}_{2}(s)+\frac{4}{{s}^{2}+4}\end{aligned}
$$

where $X_1(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_1(t) \right\}$ and $X_2(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_2(t) \right\}$ are the Laplace transforms of the functions $x_1(t)$ and $x_2(t),$ respectively." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166934 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-b4ba1928-c543-554d-8f81-96f348be498a" "question-1151a388-649e-5c91-8e65-af0ed8268c10" "question-8dcb1599-ae92-594f-a29c-09dd73cb7136" "question-4e326d04-8454-5a4c-8291-8ce0cd1c8852"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166531 :question/problem "![](images/b8/b8fb674be80033481557f5d18625e9d406934b0702f21997fcdd544ab92691ba.svg)
Consider the initial value problem above. By applying the Laplace transform $\mathcal{L}$ to both sides of each equation in our system, we get a system with variables $X_1(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_1(t) \right\}$ and $X_2(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_2(t) \right\}.$ In terms of the parameter $s,$  find the solution of the new system." :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the Laplace transforms of both sides of each equation in our system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}L\{{x}_{1}^{′}(t)\}=L\{-{x}_{1}(t)+4\} \\ L\{{x}_{2}^{′}(t)\}=L\{2{x}_{1}(t)-3{x}_{2}(t)\}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the derivative property of the Laplace transform, we obtain the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}sL\{{x}_{1}(t)\}-{x}_{1}(0)=-L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}+4L\{1\} \\ sL\{{x}_{2}(t)\}-{x}_{2}(0)=2L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}-3L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}\end{aligned}
$$

which can be simplified to the following:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)-1=-{X}_{1}(s)+\frac{4}{s} \\ s{X}_{2}(s)-0=2{X}_{1}(s)-3{X}_{2}(s)\end{aligned}
$$

where $X_1(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_1(t) \right\}$ and $X_2(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_2(t) \right\},$ and we have used the fact that $\mathcal L\{1\} = \dfrac1s.$

Now, solving the first equation for $X_1(s),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)-1 & =-{X}_{1}(s)+\frac{4}{s} \\ (s+1){X}_{1}(s) & =1+\frac{4}{s} \\ (s+1){X}_{1}(s) & =\frac{s+4}{s} \\ {X}_{1}(s) & =\frac{s+4}{s(s+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this in the second equation and solving for $X_2(s),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}s{X}_{2}(s) & =2{X}_{1}(s)-3{X}_{2}(s) \\ (s+3){X}_{2}(s) & =2{X}_{1}(s) \\ (s+3){X}_{2}(s) & =2(\frac{s+4}{s(s+1)}) \\ {X}_{2}(s) & =\frac{2(s+4)}{s(s+1)(s+3)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution of the new system in terms of parameter $s$ is 

$$
X_1(s) = \dfrac{s+4}{s(s+1)} ,\qquad 
X_2(s) = \dfrac{2(s+4)}{s(s+1)(s+3)}.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166935 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-81e3b89d-a932-5551-882e-cf97243e80bc" "question-69e91785-0e6d-5932-8b31-7b7666b19d7a" "question-80182570-5c16-548e-a977-c22b33e10f6d"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166532 :question/problem "![](images/61/61e3df899d4d41b388f160da60691aab05bd396f9826e0ea11db32780ff1ce55.svg)
Consider the initial value problem above. By applying the Laplace transform to both sides of each equation in our system, we get a transformed system with the solution 

$$
X_1(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_1(t) \right\} = -\dfrac{1}{s+2} + \dfrac{2}{s-1} - \dfrac{2}{s}, \qquad
X_2(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_2(t) \right\} = \dfrac{1}{s+2} + \dfrac{3}{s}.
$$

Find the solution to the original initial value problem." :question/worked-solution "To find $x_1(t)$ and $x_2(t)$ satisfying the original initial value problem, we apply the inverse Laplace transform to $X_1(s)$ and $X_2(s){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{{X}_{1}(s)\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{-\frac{1}{s+2}+\frac{2}{s-1}-\frac{2}{s}\} \\  & =-{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s+2}\}+2\,{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-1}\}-2\,{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s}\} \\  & =-{e}^{-2\cdot t}+2{e}^{1\cdot t}-2\cdot 1 \\  & =2{e}^{t}-{e}^{-2t}-2 \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{{X}_{2}(s)\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s+2}+\frac{3}{s}\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s+2}\}+3\,{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s}\} \\  & ={e}^{-2\cdot t}+3\cdot 1 \\  & ={e}^{-2t}+3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{t}-{e}^{-2t}-2 \\ {e}^{-2t}+3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-7ee61787-7fd7-52ae-8d70-3b4f4209ed09" :question/id #uuid "7ee61787-7fd7-52ae-8d70-3b4f4209ed09" :question/math-academy-id "q-332827" :question/problem "$$

$$

Consider the initial value problem above. By applying the Laplace transform to both sides of each equation, we get the system

$$

Finally, using the results

$$

$$

Finally, we write down the solution to the initial value problem:

$$

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186164464 :answer-field/correct "answer-c2fe2a56-87fa-54f1-8bda-525eba574bd7" :answer-field/choices ["answer-c2fe2a56-87fa-54f1-8bda-525eba574bd7"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c2fe2a56-87fa-54f1-8bda-525eba574bd7" :answer/id #uuid "c2fe2a56-87fa-54f1-8bda-525eba574bd7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "e^{t}+2e^{3t}-1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186164465 :answer-field/correct "answer-a22272d0-9fb6-5234-800e-83cf913bd389" :answer-field/choices ["answer-a22272d0-9fb6-5234-800e-83cf913bd389"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a22272d0-9fb6-5234-800e-83cf913bd389" :answer/id #uuid "a22272d0-9fb6-5234-800e-83cf913bd389" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "e^{3t}-2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168032 :tutorial/content "In this topic, we'll learn how to use Laplace transforms to solve inhomogeneous systems like the one below.
![](images/e0/e04825ebe3b670d020df9c4dad9b86564a57542effc88b77d5778f535e15d5bf.svg)

Similar to the homogeneous case, the process can be split into three steps.

- **Step 1.** Apply the Laplace transform $\mathcal{L}$ to both sides of each equation, to get a system with variables 

$$
X_1(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_1(t) \right\} \qquad \text{and} \qquad X_2(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_2(t) \right\}.
$$

- **Step 2.** Solve the obtained system for variables 

$$
X_1(s) \qquad \text{and} \qquad X_2(s).
$$

- **Step 3.** To find initial variables 

$$
x_1(t) \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_2(t)
$$

satisfying the original initial value problem, apply the inverse Laplace transform to 

$$
X_1(s) \qquad \text{and} \qquad X_2(s).
$$

Let's see how this works in practice." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186167993 :tutorial/content "![](images/0b/0bebe0003d3d70b77be931f2dba651d85352bddf6e41b94055bb227b07d60153.svg)

**Step 1**. In the initial value problem above, we apply the Laplace transform $\mathcal{L}$ to both sides of each equation.

First, we compute the Laplace transforms of both sides of each equation in our system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}L\{{x}_{1}^{′}(t)\}=L\{{x}_{1}(t)+5\} \\ L\{{x}_{2}^{′}(t)\}=L\{-2{x}_{1}(t)+4{x}_{2}(t)-2\}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the derivative property of the Laplace transform, we obtain the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}sL\{{x}_{1}(t)\}-{x}_{1}(0)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}+5L\{1\} \\ sL\{{x}_{2}(t)\}-{x}_{2}(0)=-2L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}+4L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}-2L\{1\}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the result

$$
\mathcal L\{1\} = \dfrac{1}{s},
$$

we can write our system as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)+2={X}_{1}(s)+\frac{5}{s} \\ s{X}_{2}(s)-3=-2{X}_{1}(s)+4{X}_{2}(s)-\frac{2}{s}\end{aligned}
$$

where $X_1(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_1(t) \right\}$ and $X_2(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_2(t) \right\}$ are the Laplace transforms of the functions $x_1(t)$ and $x_2(t),$ respectively.

**Step 2**. Now, solving the first equation for $X_1(s),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)+2={X}_{1}(s)+\frac{5}{s}\,⟹\,{X}_{1}(s) & =\frac{-2s+5}{s(s-1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this in the second equation and solving for $X_2(s),$ we have

$$
s X_2(s) - 3 = - 2 \left(\dfrac{-2s+5}{s(s-1)}\right) + 4 X_2(s) - \dfrac{2}{s}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
X_2(s) = \dfrac{3s^2-s-8}{s(s-1)(s-4)}.
$$

**Step 3**. To find $x_1(t)$ and $x_2(t)$ satisfying the original initial value problem, we apply the inverse Laplace transform to $X_1(s)$ and $X_2(s){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{{X}_{1}(s)\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{-2s+5}{s(s-1)}\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{3}{s-1}-\frac{5}{s}\} \\  & =3{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-1}\}-5{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s}\} \\  & =3{e}^{t}-5 \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{{X}_{2}(s)\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{3{s}^{2}-s-8}{s(s-1)(s-4)}\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{2}{s-1}+\frac{3}{s-4}-\frac{2}{s}\} \\  & =2{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-1}\}+3{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-4}\}-2{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s}\} \\  & =2{e}^{t}+3{e}^{4t}-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{t}-5 \\ 2{e}^{t}+3{e}^{4t}-2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166988 :activity/expected-seconds 1260.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

Similar to the homogeneous case, the process can be split into three steps.

- **Step 1.** Apply the Laplace transform $\mathcal{L}$ to both sides of each equation, to get a system with variables 

$$
X_1(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_1(t) \right\} \qquad \text{and} \qquad X_2(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_2(t) \right\}.
$$

- **Step 2.** Solve the obtained system for variables 

$$
X_1(s) \qquad \text{and} \qquad X_2(s).
$$

- **Step 3.** To find initial variables 

$$
x_1(t) \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_2(t)
$$

satisfying the original initial value problem, apply the inverse Laplace transform to 

$$
X_1(s) \qquad \text{and} \qquad X_2(s).
$$

Let's see how this works in practice." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186167993 :tutorial/content "![](images/0b/0bebe0003d3d70b77be931f2dba651d85352bddf6e41b94055bb227b07d60153.svg)

**Step 1**. In the initial value problem above, we apply the Laplace transform $\mathcal{L}$ to both sides of each equation.

First, we compute the Laplace transforms of both sides of each equation in our system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}L\{{x}_{1}^{′}(t)\}=L\{{x}_{1}(t)+5\} \\ L\{{x}_{2}^{′}(t)\}=L\{-2{x}_{1}(t)+4{x}_{2}(t)-2\}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the derivative property of the Laplace transform, we obtain the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}sL\{{x}_{1}(t)\}-{x}_{1}(0)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}+5L\{1\} \\ sL\{{x}_{2}(t)\}-{x}_{2}(0)=-2L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}+4L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}-2L\{1\}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the result

$$
\mathcal L\{1\} = \dfrac{1}{s},
$$

we can write our system as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)+2={X}_{1}(s)+\frac{5}{s} \\ s{X}_{2}(s)-3=-2{X}_{1}(s)+4{X}_{2}(s)-\frac{2}{s}\end{aligned}
$$

where $X_1(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_1(t) \right\}$ and $X_2(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_2(t) \right\}$ are the Laplace transforms of the functions $x_1(t)$ and $x_2(t),$ respectively.

**Step 2**. Now, solving the first equation for $X_1(s),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)+2={X}_{1}(s)+\frac{5}{s}\,⟹\,{X}_{1}(s) & =\frac{-2s+5}{s(s-1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this in the second equation and solving for $X_2(s),$ we have

$$
s X_2(s) - 3 = - 2 \left(\dfrac{-2s+5}{s(s-1)}\right) + 4 X_2(s) - \dfrac{2}{s}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
X_2(s) = \dfrac{3s^2-s-8}{s(s-1)(s-4)}.
$$

**Step 3**. To find $x_1(t)$ and $x_2(t)$ satisfying the original initial value problem, we apply the inverse Laplace transform to $X_1(s)$ and $X_2(s){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{{X}_{1}(s)\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{-2s+5}{s(s-1)}\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{3}{s-1}-\frac{5}{s}\} \\  & =3{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-1}\}-5{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s}\} \\  & =3{e}^{t}-5 \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{{X}_{2}(s)\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{3{s}^{2}-s-8}{s(s-1)(s-4)}\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{2}{s-1}+\frac{3}{s-4}-\frac{2}{s}\} \\  & =2{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-1}\}+3{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-4}\}-2{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s}\} \\  & =2{e}^{t}+3{e}^{4t}-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{t}-5 \\ 2{e}^{t}+3{e}^{4t}-2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=2{x}_{1}(t)+2{e}^{-t} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)={x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}(t)+3,\end{aligned}\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the initial value problem above. By applying the Laplace transform to both sides of each equation, we get the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{{field-1}}=2{X}_{1}(s)+{{field-2}} \\ s{X}_{2}(s)+1={X}_{1}(s)+{X}_{2}(s)+{{field-3}}\end{aligned}
$$

where ${X}_{1}(s)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}$ and ${X}_{2}(s)=L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}$ are the Laplace transforms of the functions ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t),$ respectively."] ["question-66762fbf-e11e-5167-966c-39877463d24c" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the Laplace transforms of both sides of each equation in our system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}L\{{x}_{1}^{′}(t)\}=L\{2{x}_{1}(t)+2{e}^{-t}\} \\ L\{{x}_{2}^{′}(t)\}=L\{{x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}(t)+3\}\end{aligned}\,\,
$$

Using the derivative property of the Laplace transform, we obtain the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}sL\{{x}_{1}(t)\}-{x}_{1}(0)=2L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}+2L\{{e}^{-t}\} \\ sL\{{x}_{2}(t)\}-{x}_{2}(0)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}+L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}+3L\{1\}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the results

$$
L\{1\}=\frac{1}{s},\,L\{{e}^{-t}\}=\frac{1}{s+1},
$$

we can write our system as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)=2{X}_{1}(s)+\frac{2}{s+1} \\ s{X}_{2}(s)+1={X}_{1}(s)+{X}_{2}(s)+\frac{3}{s}\end{aligned}
$$

where ${X}_{1}(s)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}$ and ${X}_{2}(s)=L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}$ are the Laplace transforms of the functions ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t),$ respectively."] $$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)+3=-2{X}_{1}(s) \\ s{X}_{2}(s)-1=3{X}_{1}(s)+4{X}_{2}(s)+\frac{5}{s}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}sL\{{x}_{1}(t)\}-{x}_{1}(0)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}+5L\{1\} \\ sL\{{x}_{2}(t)\}-{x}_{2}(0)=-2L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}+4L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}-2L\{1\}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the result

$$
\mathcal L\{1\} = \dfrac{1}{s},
$$

we can write our system as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)+2={X}_{1}(s)+\frac{5}{s} \\ s{X}_{2}(s)-3=-2{X}_{1}(s)+4{X}_{2}(s)-\frac{2}{s}\end{aligned}
$$

where $X_1(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_1(t) \right\}$ and $X_2(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_2(t) \right\}$ are the Laplace transforms of the functions $x_1(t)$ and $x_2(t),$ respectively.

**Step 2**. Now, solving the first equation for $X_1(s),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)+2={X}_{1}(s)+\frac{5}{s}\,⟹\,{X}_{1}(s) & =\frac{-2s+5}{s(s-1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this in the second equation and solving for $X_2(s),$ we have

$$
s X_2(s) - 3 = - 2 \left(\dfrac{-2s+5}{s(s-1)}\right) + 4 X_2(s) - \dfrac{2}{s}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad

$$

$$

$$

$$

- **Step 2.** Solve the obtained system for variables 

$$
X_1(s) \qquad \text{and} \qquad X_2(s).
$$

- **Step 3.** To find initial variables 

$$
x_1(t) \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_2(t)

{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{'}(t)={x}_{1}(t)+5 \\ {x}_{2}^{'}(t)=-2{x}_{1}(t)+4{x}_{2}(t)-2,\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 1**. In the initial value problem above, we apply the Laplace transform $\mathcal{L}$ to both sides of each equation.

First, we compute the Laplace transforms of both sides of each equation in our system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}L{{x}_{1}^{'}(t)}=L{{x}_{1}(t)+5} \\ L{{x}_{2}^{'}(t)}=L{-2{x}_{1}(t)+4{x}_{2}(t)-2}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the derivative property of the Laplace transform, we obtain the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}sL{{x}_{1}(t)}-{x}_{1}(0)=L{{x}_{1}(t)}+5L{1} \\ sL{{x}_{2}(t)}-{x}_{2}(0)=-2L{{x}_{1}(t)}+4L{{x}_{2}(t)}-2L{1}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the result

$$
\mathcal L\{1\} = \dfrac{1}{s},
$$

we can write our system as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)+2={X}_{1}(s)+\frac{5}{s} \\ s{X}_{2}(s)-3=-2{X}_{1}(s)+4{X}_{2}(s)-\frac{2}{s}\end{aligned}
$$

where $X_1(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_1(t) \right\}$ and $X_2(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_2(t) \right\}$ are the Laplace transforms of the functions $x_1(t)$ and $x_2(t),$ respectively.

**Step 2**. Now, solving the first equation for $X_1(s),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)+2={X}_{1}(s)+\frac{5}{s}\,⟹\,{X}_{1}(s) & =\frac{-2s+5}{s(s-1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this in the second equation and solving for $X_2(s),$ we have

$$
s X_2(s) - 3 = - 2 \left(\dfrac{-2s+5}{s(s-1)}\right) + 4 X_2(s) - \dfrac{2}{s}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
X_2(s) = \dfrac{3s^2-s-8}{s(s-1)(s-4)}.
$$

**Step 3**. To find $x_1(t)$ and $x_2(t)$ satisfying the original initial value problem, we apply the inverse Laplace transform to $X_1(s)$ and $X_2(s){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & ={L}^{-1}{{X}_{1}(s)} \\  & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{-2s+5}{s(s-1)}} \\  & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{3}{s-1}-\frac{5}{s}} \\  & =3{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s-1}}-5{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s}} \\  & =3{e}^{t}-5 \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={L}^{-1}{{X}_{2}(s)} \\  & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{3{s}^{2}-s-8}{s(s-1)(s-4)}} \\  & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{2}{s-1}+\frac{3}{s-4}-\frac{2}{s}} \\  & =2{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s-1}}+3{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s-4}}-2{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s}} \\  & =2{e}^{t}+3{e}^{4t}-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{t}-5 \\ 2{e}^{t}+3{e}^{4t}-2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"]]}

$$

Using the derivative property of the Laplace transform, we obtain the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}sL{{x}_{1}(t)}-{x}_{1}(0)=-L{{x}_{1}(t)}+4L{1} \\ sL{{x}_{2}(t)}-{x}_{2}(0)=2L{{x}_{1}(t)}-3L{{x}_{2}(t)}\end{aligned}
$$

which can be simplified to the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)-1=-{X}_{1}(s)+\frac{4}{s} \\ s{X}_{2}(s)-0=2{X}_{1}(s)-3{X}_{2}(s)\end{aligned}
$$

where $X_1(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_1(t) \right\}$ and $X_2(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_2(t) \right\},$ and we have used the fact that $\mathcal L\{1\} = \dfrac1s.$

Now, solving the first equation for $X_1(s),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)-1 & =-{X}_{1}(s)+\frac{4}{s} \\ (s+1){X}_{1}(s) & =1+\frac{4}{s} \\ (s+1){X}_{1}(s) & =\frac{s+4}{s} \\ {X}_{1}(s) & =\frac{s+4}{s(s+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this in the second equation and solving for $X_2(s),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}s{X}_{2}(s) & =2{X}_{1}(s)-3{X}_{2}(s) \\ (s+3){X}_{2}(s) & =2{X}_{1}(s) \\ (s+3){X}_{2}(s) & =2(\frac{s+4}{s(s+1)}) \\ {X}_{2}(s) & =\frac{2(s+4)}{s(s+1)(s+3)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution of the new system in terms of parameter $s$ is 

$$

:activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186167891 :step/content {:db/id 17592186167993 :tutorial/content "$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{'}(t)={x}_{1}(t)+5 \\ {x}_{2}^{'}(t)=-2{x}_{1}(t)+4{x}_{2}(t)-2,\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 1**. In the initial value problem above, we apply the Laplace transform $\mathcal{L}$ to both sides of each equation.

First, we compute the Laplace transforms of both sides of each equation in our system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}L{{x}_{1}^{'}(t)}=L{{x}_{1}(t)+5} \\ L{{x}_{2}^{'}(t)}=L{-2{x}_{1}(t)+4{x}_{2}(t)-2}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the derivative property of the Laplace transform, we obtain the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}sL{{x}_{1}(t)}-{x}_{1}(0)=L{{x}_{1}(t)}+5L{1} \\ sL{{x}_{2}(t)}-{x}_{2}(0)=-2L{{x}_{1}(t)}+4L{{x}_{2}(t)}-2L{1}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the result

$$
\mathcal L\{1\} = \dfrac{1}{s},
$$

we can write our system as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)+2={X}_{1}(s)+\frac{5}{s} \\ s{X}_{2}(s)-3=-2{X}_{1}(s)+4{X}_{2}(s)-\frac{2}{s}\end{aligned}
$$

where $X_1(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_1(t) \right\}$ and $X_2(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_2(t) \right\}$ are the Laplace transforms of the functions $x_1(t)$ and $x_2(t),$ respectively.

**Step 2**. Now, solving the first equation for $X_1(s),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)+2={X}_{1}(s)+\frac{5}{s}\,⟹\,{X}_{1}(s) & =\frac{-2s+5}{s(s-1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this in the second equation and solving for $X_2(s),$ we have

$$
s X_2(s) - 3 = - 2 \left(\dfrac{-2s+5}{s(s-1)}\right) + 4 X_2(s) - \dfrac{2}{s}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
X_2(s) = \dfrac{3s^2-s-8}{s(s-1)(s-4)}.
$$

**Step 3**. To find $x_1(t)$ and $x_2(t)$ satisfying the original initial value problem, we apply the inverse Laplace transform to $X_1(s)$ and $X_2(s){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & ={L}^{-1}{{X}_{1}(s)} \\  & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{-2s+5}{s(s-1)}} \\  & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{3}{s-1}-\frac{5}{s}} \\  & =3{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s-1}}-5{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s}} \\  & =3{e}^{t}-5 \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={L}^{-1}{{X}_{2}(s)} \\  & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{3{s}^{2}-s-8}{s(s-1)(s-4)}} \\  & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{2}{s-1}+\frac{3}{s-4}-\frac{2}{s}} \\  & =2{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s-1}}+3{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s-4}}-2{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s}} \\  & =2{e}^{t}+3{e}^{4t}-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{t}-5 \\ 2{e}^{t}+3{e}^{4t}-2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "00904ad0-6191-560b-a452-c838aa7543a6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14420 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "822d22ea-2253-5461-b518-1ae1ae238fee" {:db/id 17592186167895 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168032 :tutorial/content "In this topic, we'll learn how to use Laplace transforms to solve inhomogeneous systems like the one below.

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{'}(t)={x}_{1}(t)+5 \\ {x}_{2}^{'}(t)=-2{x}_{1}(t)+4{x}_{2}(t)-2,\end{aligned}
$$

Similar to the homogeneous case, the process can be split into three steps.

- **Step 1.** Apply the Laplace transform $\mathcal{L}$ to both sides of each equation, to get a system with variables 

$$
X_1(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_1(t) \right\} \qquad \text{and} \qquad X_2(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_2(t) \right\}.
$$

- **Step 2.** Solve the obtained system for variables 

$$
X_1(s) \qquad \text{and} \qquad X_2(s).
$$

- **Step 3.** To find initial variables 

$$
x_1(t) \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_2(t)
$$

satisfying the original initial value problem, apply the inverse Laplace transform to 

$$
X_1(s) \qquad \text{and} \qquad X_2(s).
$$

Let's see how this works in practice." :tutorial/id #uuid "3733acd7-1a13-5183-a501-0baf1eaf53a5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14611 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "91a3017f-8462-5088-8b1f-303f10ce818d" :step/math-academy-id 590715 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167891}}] :activity/title "Solving Inhomogeneous Systems of ODEs Using Laplace Transforms" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186166988} {:db/id 17592186167895 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168032 :tutorial/content "In this topic, we'll learn how to use Laplace transforms to solve inhomogeneous systems like the one below.

"5d6348a1-6da4-5516-b665-5319df7cd619" :step/math-academy-id 590712} {:db/id 17592186168032 :tutorial/content "In this topic, we'll learn how to use Laplace transforms to solve inhomogeneous systems like the one below.

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{'}(t)={x}_{1}(t)+5 \\ {x}_{2}^{'}(t)=-2{x}_{1}(t)+4{x}_{2}(t)-2,\end{aligned}
$$

Similar to the homogeneous case, the process can be split into three steps.

- **Step 1.** Apply the Laplace transform $\mathcal{L}$ to both sides of each equation, to get a system with variables 

$$
X_1(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_1(t) \right\} \qquad \text{and} \qquad X_2(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_2(t) \right\}.
$$

- **Step 2.** Solve the obtained system for variables 

$$
X_1(s) \qquad \text{and} \qquad X_2(s).
$$

- **Step 3.** To find initial variables 

$$
x_1(t) \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_2(t)
$$

satisfying the original initial value problem, apply the inverse Laplace transform to 

$$
X_1(s) \qquad \text{and} \qquad X_2(s).
$$

Let's see how this works in practice." :tutorial/id #uuid "3733acd7-1a13-5183-a501-0baf1eaf53a5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14611 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident Students study norms, inner products, orthogonality, and orthogonal complements in vector spaces over the real and complex numbers. Techniques such as orthogonal projections, the Gram–Schmidt process, and QR factorization allow vectors to be decomposed into orthogonal components. These ideas play a role in Fourier analysis, signal decomposition, and numerical methods used in physical simulations.
Students then explore quadratic forms and the diagonalization of symmetric matrices. The spectral theorem provides a geometric interpretation of symmetric transformations and leads to techniques for analyzing energy functions and stability in physical systems. Singular value decomposition is also introduced as a powerful matrix factorization with applications in numerical modeling and data analysis.
Applications of linear algebra follow, including least-squares methods for solving overdetermined systems. These methods arise when fitting theoretical models to experimental data and when approximating solutions to physical equations.
The course then develops multivariable integration in three dimensions. Students compute triple integrals over general regions and apply coordinate transformations such as cylindrical and spherical coordinates. These techniques allow physicists to compute quantities such as mass distributions, charge densities, and gravitational or electric potentials.
Students next study line integrals and surface integrals of scalar and vector fields. Concepts such as circulation, flux, and path independence lead to the fundamental theorems of vector calculus, including Green’s theorem, the divergence theorem, and Stokes’ theorem. These results form the mathematical framework underlying conservation laws and the differential and integral formulations of electromagnetic theory.
Applications of multivariable calculus follow, including vector mechanics and optimization. Students analyze motion using vector-valued functions, apply Newton’s second law to systems in the plane, and study work–energy relationships. Multiple integrals are used to compute mass, centers of mass, moments of inertia, and other physical quantities.
The course then returns to differential equations, extending earlier techniques to systems of linear differential equations. Students analyze dynamical systems using eigenvalues, phase portraits, and matrix methods, which appear in models of interacting systems such as coupled oscillators or predator–prey dynamics.
Laplace transforms are introduced as a powerful tool for solving linear differential equations with discontinuous inputs or initial conditions. Boundary value problems and Fourier series are then developed, providing mathematical techniques used to solve differential equations describing heat flow, vibrating strings, wave propagation, and other physical phenomena.
The course concludes with numerical methods for differential equations and advanced probability topics.
